questions.narration: Three students are discussing struggling with academic writing at university.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: I’m finding academic writing so tough this semester. I just can’t seem to get my ideas across clearly on paper, and my grades are suffering. I think it’s the structure that gets me the most. I end up rambling and never really making a solid point. It’s frustrating because I understand the material, I just can't articulate it well.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: I totally get that. For me, it’s the research. Finding credible sources and then, like, putting them into my writing without plagiarizing is a nightmare. I spend more time worrying about citations than actually writing the paper. And honestly, just understanding what counts as 'good' research is half the battle, you know?

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: You both hit on my biggest struggles! But I also think about how much there is to do. It feels like every class needs a massive research paper. Trying to balance that with everything else, like exams and stuff, is impossible. I start procrastinating because it feels so overwhelming, and then I end up rushing and doing a bad job.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Maybe we should look into the writing center? I've heard mixed reviews, but it could be worth a shot. They offer workshops on things like structuring essays and, you know, proper citation, which might help us both, Chris. Or, we could form a study group and read each other's papers before we hand them in. Fresh eyes can often catch things we miss ourselves.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: I'm down for a study group! I've been meaning to try that. The writing center sounds good too, although I worry it'll be super busy so close to the deadline. I did hear from a friend that the library has research skills workshops. Maybe focusing on finding better sources could take some of the pressure off.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: I'm in on both! A study group would definitely help with feeling so overwhelmed. Just having someone to bounce ideas off of could make a huge difference. And anything that makes my research better is a win. I'll check out the library workshops, and Sarah, maybe you can check out the writing center?

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Deal! I'll look into the writing center and tell you what I find out. We could even set specific goals for our study group sessions, like outlining an essay or proofreading, like, a certain number of pages. Having a structured approach might make it less scary.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: That sounds like a solid plan. I think breaking down the writing process into smaller steps will make a huge difference. I'm actually feeling more optimistic already! Plus, misery loves company, right? It's good to know we're all in the same boat.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: Absolutely! And knowing we're actually working on getting better is a huge confidence booster. I'm actually excited to start the next paper now. Let's figure out our schedules and get this study group going!

questions.narration: Two students and a professor are discussing experiences in large vs small lectures at university.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: I really prefer small lectures, honestly. In a big lecture hall, I just feel like I'm just another face, and it's hard to really get involved. I find myself kind of zoning out a lot more easily when there are hundreds of other students around.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: That's interesting, because I actually prefer big lectures because I like being anonymous. I like just being able to sit there, take notes, and, you know, just take in the information without feeling like I have to speak up or anything. Plus, they often have really good stuff, like clear slides and sometimes they even record the sessions, which is super helpful when you're revising.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: It's true that big lectures are often really important for, like, the basic courses, especially when there are a lot of students. They help us teach the main stuff effectively to many students. But, I do miss how you can really interact in a smaller class. It's just easier to see if everyone understands and to have more discussions where people talk to each other.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Exactly! In a big lecture, if you have a quick question, you can't just shout it out, and raising your hand feels awkward with so many eyes on you. You just end up waiting until after class, if you even remember, or you just stay confused. It really makes it harder for me to learn.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: I guess I just don't have that problem as much. A lot of my big lectures have specific times for questions, or even online forums that the TAs run where you can just ask questions without anyone knowing who you are. I think that works pretty well for clearing things up without stopping the main lecture.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: That's a good point about using technology and having enough staff to help out. We're always trying to find ways to make those big classes more interactive. It's really about finding a balance between getting information out to everyone and making sure every student feels supported as they learn.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Maybe if big lectures had more interactive parts, like in-class polls or quick things to discuss, that would really help. Even putting us into small groups for a couple of minutes to talk about something could make a huge difference. That way, you're not just sitting there and listening for an hour.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: I totally agree with adding more interactive parts to big lectures; that would definitely make things better. But for some subjects, like really big introductory science classes, you really need to get that general idea first before you go into all the details. Small lectures just wouldn't be able to cover so much information as well.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: You've both brought up some really important points. I think the best way is probably to have a mix of both. So, big lectures for the basic ideas, and then smaller tutorials or seminars for, like, deeper talks and more personal feedback. It's about setting up the learning so it really fits the subject and what students need, and also using technology to make it more engaging.

questions.narration: Three students are discussing whether to restrict students' phone use on campus.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Hey guys, did you hear Professor Wang is pushing for phone restrictions in class and the library? I’m all for it! Last week in math class, half the people were scrolling TikTok under their desks—Professor had to stop teaching three times to remind us. If phones are banned, we’d actually focus, and I bet my grades would go up.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: Totally agree! I was in the library yesterday trying to write a paper, but the girl next to me kept taking video calls—so annoying! Phones are such a distraction; I even catch myself checking messages when I’m supposed to be studying. Restrictions would help us stay on track, and maybe we’d talk more with classmates instead of staring at screens.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: Wait, isn’t that too strict? What if there’s an emergency? My mom has a heart condition, and she needs to reach me anytime. Last month, she had to go to the hospital, and she texted me during class—I would’ve panicked if I didn’t see it. Plus, phones are useful for studying!

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: I get the emergency part, but maybe we could keep phones on silent and only use them outside if needed? Like, step out of class to take a call. And for studying—flashcards are great, but do you really need your phone the whole time?

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: Exactly! Emergencies are rare, and stepping out solves that. As for study apps, you could use them before class or during breaks instead of in the library. My cousin’s school has phone lockers in classrooms—you put your phone in at the start, get it back after. She said it was weird at first, but now she loves how focused everyone is.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: Hmm, lockers sound okay, but what about when I need to use my phone for class? Last week, Professor Li had us look up an article on our phones during lecture. If they’re locked up, we can’t do that. And what if I forget something at home? I text my roommate to bring it, which I can’t do if my phone’s restricted.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Oh, right—class uses! Maybe the rule could be “no non-study phone use” instead of total restriction? Like, you can use it for articles or apps the professor assigns, but no scrolling. That way, you still have it for emergencies and school stuff, but not distractions.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: That makes sense! My friend’s class has that rule—Professor walks around, and if you’re on social media, you have to put your phone away. It works because it’s not a total ban, just limits the bad stuff. We could suggest that to Professor Wang—she’s always asking for student input.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: Thanks, guys—I was worried about emergencies, but “no non-study use” fixes that. I’ll even try putting my phone on “do not disturb” during study time this week to test it. Let’s talk to Professor Wang together tomorrow—maybe we can help make a rule that works for everyone!

questions.narration: Three students are discussing joining the debating club at university.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: I've been thinking about joining the debating club for a while now. It seems like a great way to get better at public speaking and thinking critically. But I'm also a little nervous, 'cause I've never really done proper debating before. I'm worried about having to think up arguments really fast and, like, saying them well. Has anyone here ever done debating?

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: I did a bit of debating in high school, and it was really good. It definitely helped me be more confident when I say what I think and when I have to think fast. The thing is, it does take a lot of prep and, like, looking stuff up, which can take time. You have to be ready to work hard to know your stuff and make good arguments. But honestly, it's worth it.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: I agree with Will. I haven't done formal debates, but I've seen how good it can be. I want to join because I think it would help me see things from different points of view. I think it’s important to be able to talk things through properly, even if you don't agree with someone. Plus, I've heard the club does workshops and practice for beginners, so you don't just get thrown in at the deep end.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: It's good to know about the workshops, Laura. I'm still a bit worried about the competition side of things. Do you have to be, like, super competitive to do well in the club? I'm more interested in learning and getting better, rather than winning all the time. Also, I'm a bit worried I won't have enough time because of my courses.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: Yeah, some people are really competitive, but the club also cares about learning and getting better. You can do less formal debates and practice where it's more about improving your skills, not just winning. And you don't have to do everything; you can pick what fits your schedule and what you like. It's all about finding what's good for you.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: Exactly! And think about the networking! Debating can help you get internships, scholarships, even jobs. Employers often want people who can communicate well and think critically, which you'll learn in the club. I think it's a great investment in your future, even if you don't want to be a professional debater.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: Laura, that's a really good point about the networking. I didn't think of that. But yeah, meeting people who are into the same things and getting to know experienced debaters could be really useful. Maybe we should all check out the club's next meeting and see what it's like. We can help each other out.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: That sounds great, Will! I feel much better about trying it now. It'll be less scary with you both there. Plus, I'm excited about meeting new people and, like, seeing new things. Let's look at the club's website and find out when the next meeting is. Maybe we can get coffee first and talk about what we want to get out of joining.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: Perfect! I'm looking forward to it. I've heard they're having a social thing soon too, which would be a fun way to meet everyone in a more relaxed way. I'm sure it'll be in the student union, so it'll be easy to get to. Let’s definitely do some research before the first meeting, so we can get a feel of what the club's like, and maybe think of some topics we could debate.

questions.topic: Debate on replacing traditional exams with project-based assessments
questions.narration: Three students are sitting on the grass near the library, discussing a proposal to replace traditional final exams with project-based assessments in some courses.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: I think project-based assessments are much better than exams. In my marketing class last semester, we had to create a full campaign for a local business. I learned more from that project than from any exam. It felt practical and relevant.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: I see the appeal, but projects can be stressful too. They take weeks to complete, and group projects often have problems with unequal contribution. Plus, some subjects like mathematics or chemistry really need exams to test quick recall and problem-solving under time pressure.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: That's true for some subjects, but for many others, projects allow you to demonstrate deeper understanding. You can research, apply concepts, and show creativity. Exams just test memorization.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: I think a mix would be ideal. Some courses could have a project component worth, say, 40 percent of the grade, with a shorter exam for the rest. That way, you get the benefits of both. It also reduces the pressure of a single high-stakes exam.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: That could work. But we'd need clear rubrics for projects to ensure fair grading. I've had projects where the grading felt arbitrary.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: Yes, rubrics are essential. They should be provided at the start so students know exactly what is expected.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: I agree. And projects should be individual whenever possible to avoid the free-rider problem in group work.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: That would increase the workload for professors, though. Grading thirty individual projects takes much more time than grading one exam.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: The university could allocate more teaching assistant hours to help with grading. It's an investment in better assessment.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Let's propose a pilot program in a few departments, like humanities and social sciences, where projects are more natural. If successful, it could be expanded.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: I could support that. Let's gather examples from other universities that have done this successfully.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: Good plan. I'll start researching best practices for project-based assessment rubrics.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Also, we should consider that projects often require students to manage their time over several weeks, which is a valuable skill for the workplace.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: That is a good point. Time management is indeed important.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: And we could design projects that include both individual and group components, so students learn collaboration as well as independent work.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Exactly. That way, the assessment mirrors real-world tasks more closely.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: I think we should also look at how other universities handle the grading workload. Some use peer review sessions to reduce the burden on professors.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: That's a great idea. Peer review could also help students learn from each other.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Let's include peer review in our proposal.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: I'll draft a section on grading workload solutions.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: And I'll compile examples of successful project-based assessment implementations from other institutions.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: So, I've been trying out different ways to take notes lately, and I'm not really sure which one works best. I tried the Cornell method, but it feels a little too structured for me, you know? What about you guys, what do you usually do?

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: I'm a big fan of mind mapping, actually. It really helps me see how all the ideas connect and get the bigger picture. I usually start with the main idea in the middle and then branch out from there. Plus, it's not as linear as regular note-taking, which keeps me way more interested. It’s especially helpful in subjects where things are really connected, like history or philosophy.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: I’ve tried mind mapping before, but I think it’s a bit messy, to be honest. I usually prefer outlining. It’s just simple and easy, and it helps me keep everything organized logically. I use different headings and subheadings to structure my notes, which makes it easy to look back at them later.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Yeah, I get why you'd like outlining, but sometimes I feel like I'm just writing down exactly what the professor says without really thinking about it. turns.speaker: Speaker 2

turns.speaker: Speaker 3

turns.speaker: Speaker 1

questions.narration: Three students are sitting on the campus lawn, talking about whether the school should reduce the number of campus club activities.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Ugh, I’m so exhausted this week! I had three club meetings, a debate competition for the speech club, and a volunteer event for the community service club—all after classes. I really think the school should cut down on club activities.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: Wait, I totally disagree. Club activities are the best part of school for me! I’m in the photography club, and last week we went on a field trip to the city’s art museum—we learned so much about lighting and composition, stuff I’d never get in regular classes. If the school reduces clubs, we’ll lose all these cool learning opportunities that make school more fun.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: It’s not that clubs are bad—it’s that there are too many, and they demand too much time. I joined the drama club because I love acting, but now we have rehearsals four nights a week, plus we have to build sets on weekends. My math grade dropped last month because I didn’t have time to study for the test.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Exactly! And it’s not just the time—there’s so much pressure to “be active” for college applications. My counselor said I need to “show commitment” to clubs, so I feel like I can’t quit even when I’m overwhelmed. If there were fewer activities, we could actually focus on the ones we really care about instead of spreading ourselves thin.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: But what about students who don’t have other ways to explore their interests? My friend is shy, and she only made friends because she joined the book club—they meet once a week to talk about novels, and it’s low-pressure.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: That sounds good in theory, but in reality, the club leaders always make you feel guilty if you skip something. Last week, I missed drama rehearsal because I had a doctor’s appointment, and the director kept asking me, “Do you even care about the play?”

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Maybe the solution isn’t “cut all clubs”—but just limit how many events each club can have? Like, each club can only have one meeting a week and one event a month. That way, we can still enjoy clubs without feeling swamped. I’d actually be more engaged if I didn’t have to rush to five things a week.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: Hmm, that’s a good point. I don’t want to lose the photography club’s field trips, but I get that some people are overwhelmed. Maybe the school could let students “opt in” to events instead of making them mandatory? Like, if the drama club has a set-building day, it’s optional—you can go if you have time, but you won’t get in trouble if you don’t. That way, everyone gets to choose what works for them.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: That sounds fair! I just don’t want to have to quit the drama club because it’s taking over my life. If they did rehearsals twice a week instead of four, I could balance acting and studying.

questions.narration: Three students are walking to the gym for their PE class, discussing whether the school should cancel the PE proficiency test as a graduation requirement.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Ugh, I’m so stressed about the upcoming 1000-meter run test! No matter how much I practice, I can never meet the passing standard. Why should I risk not graduating just because I’m not good at running?

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: I totally agree! I have a knee injury from last year’s basketball game, and even walking for a long time hurts, let alone running or doing pull-ups. If it’s no longer a graduation requirement, students with injuries or physical limitations won’t have to worry about their academic future being affected by something they can’t control.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: Wait, hold on—I don’t think canceling the PE proficiency test is a good idea. PE class is supposed to encourage us to stay active, and the test is a way to make sure we’re keeping up with basic fitness. Without it, a lot of students would just skip PE and become less healthy, which isn’t good for our long-term well-being.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: But the test doesn’t encourage fitness—it just makes people anxious! I have a friend who starved herself for a week before the weight and BMI test because she was scared of failing. That way, we stay active without the stress of passing a strict test.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: Yeah, and not everyone is good at traditional sports like running or swimming. I love dancing, and I practice it every weekend, but the PE test doesn’t count that as fitness. Also, the test only checks one moment of fitness, not our overall lifestyle—what’s the point of that?

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: But basic fitness is important for everyone, even if you don’t like sports. Being able to run a short distance or do a few push-ups helps with daily life—like carrying heavy books or walking up stairs. And if the school makes exceptions for students with injuries, like letting them do modified exercises, then the test can still work without being unfair.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Hmm, I get what you’re saying about basic fitness, but exceptions are hard to get. Maybe the school could replace the proficiency test with a “fitness portfolio”—we track our own physical activities over the semester, like how many times we work out, and get credit for consistency instead of a single test.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: That’s a great idea! A fitness portfolio would let us choose what activities we like, and it focuses on effort instead of results. Also, it teaches us to be responsible for our own fitness, which is a better lesson than just passing a test.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: Okay, that does sound more reasonable than just canceling the test entirely. The school could ask us to submit photos or videos of our workouts, or have PE teachers check in with us regularly. If they do that, then the portfolio could work as a fair replacement.

questions.narration: Three students are discussing preparing for an oral presentation at university.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Okay, so we're all set for our presentation next week, right? I'm feeling a bit overwhelmed, to be honest. I’ve started drafting my slides, but I’m not sure if I’m focusing on the right things, you know? I'm also worried about the time limit; it’s tough to get everything into just ten minutes. Has anyone got any tips for, like, how to structure it well?

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: Definitely! I think the key thing is to start with a really good opening that grabs everyone's attention. Then, break your main points down into smaller chunks, easier to handle. Don't try to put too much stuff on each slide. I think using visuals, like graphs or images, really helps keep people interested. And the most important thing is practice, practice! You don't want to be, like, stumbling over your words on the day.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: I agree with Liam about practicing for sure. I usually record myself giving the presentation, and then I watch it back to see where I can make it better. It’s awful, but it really does help! For the content, I think it's good to start by outlining your main arguments, even before you make the slides. What’s the main thing you're trying to say? It's easy to get lost in the details, but that'll help you stay on track.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: That’s a really good idea, Laura, about doing the outline first. I usually just jump right into the details and then I have trouble making it all make sense together. I'm also a bit nervous about the Q&A part afterwards. What if I don’t know an answer? Any ideas on how to get ready for that?

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: The Q&A is tricky, but you can get ready! Think about the questions people might ask and have some answers ready, even if they're just rough. It’s also okay to say you don’t know, but you’ll find out. Being honest is always best. Just try to, like, engage with them and show that you're thinking about the topic. Don't freak out if you get stuck; it happens to everyone!

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: I actually think the Q&A is the most fun! It's a chance to really talk with the audience and show how much you care about the topic. Going along with what Liam said, it's totally fine to say, 'That's a great question, but I don't really have a good answer right now.' You could even ask the audience what they think. It's a conversation, not, like, a test!

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Okay, I feel a bit better now. Thanks, you two! I think I’ll try to make a really good outline and practice how I'm going to say it. I'll also try to think of some questions they might ask, but I won't worry about it too much. I guess the main thing is to be ready, but also be able to change if I need to and, you know, enjoy it. That's easier said than done, though!

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: You've got this, Sarah! We're all in the same boat. Just remember to breathe and try to have fun. It's a great chance to share what you know and get some feedback. Plus, giving presentations is a really good skill to have for jobs later, so think of it as practice for after university!

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: Exactly! And don't be afraid to ask for help if you need it. We can all practice our presentations together and, like, give each other feedback. It's much easier when you know people are there for you. Let’s try to meet up again before the presentation to go over everything one last time.

questions.narration: Three students are sitting on the school lawn during break, talking about whether students should be allowed to bring phones to class.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Guys, did you hear Mr. Wang say some teachers want to ban phones in class? I totally disagree with that! Phones can be super useful for learning. Last week, when we were talking about rainforests in biology, I quickly looked up a video of Amazon wildlife on my phone and showed the whole group—it made the lesson way more interesting than just reading the textbook.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: Are you serious? Phones are such a distraction! I sit next to Lily, and she’s always scrolling through social media under her desk during math class. Last week, she even missed the teacher’s explanation of the key formula, and then she had to ask me for help after class. If phones are allowed, most students won’t use them for learning—they’ll just use them to chat or play games.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: I get where both of you are coming from, but honestly, I think we should ban phones in class too. It’s not just about distraction for the person using the phone—it’s for everyone else. Last Tuesday, someone’s phone rang during history class, and the whole room turned to look. The teacher had to stop talking for five minutes to calm everyone down. That breaks the flow of the lesson, and it’s unfair to the students who are trying to focus.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: But you can put phones in silence! My teacher has us keep phones in bags on silent, only taking them out for learning—like looking up definitions or app quizzes. Last month, we used a literature quiz app that was way more fun than paper.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: Even on silent, people get tempted! I’ve seen students sneak texts under desks, even with the teacher nearby. Important messages from parents can wait for break—class time is for listening, not checking phones.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: Speaker1, I know phones have good uses, but let’s be real—most students aren’t responsible enough. My little brother’s class tried the "silent phone in bag" rule, but half used phones secretly. The teacher had to ban them to keep class organized.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Hmm, maybe some students aren’t responsible. But why punish those who are? Maybe teachers could collect phones at the start and give them back at the end—keeping distractions away while letting responsible students use phones for learning.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: That’s a good idea! My cousin’s school uses a front-of-class phone box. If someone needs a phone for a lesson, the teacher gives it temporarily, and their class average went up last year.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: Yeah, that makes sense! Collecting phones keeps distractions away but lets us use them when needed. We should suggest this to our class teacher—she’s always asking for ways to improve class.

questions.narration: Three students are sitting on the grass outside the lecture hall, debating whether professors should ban laptops in class.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: I just heard that Professor Chen is thinking of banning laptops in his history lectures. He says students get distracted and don't pay attention. I actually agree with him. Last week, I sat next to a guy who was watching a basketball game during the lecture. It's so distracting for everyone around.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: But I rely on my laptop for note-taking. I type faster than I write, and my handwriting is terrible. Plus, I can organize my notes digitally and search them later. A ban would hurt my learning.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: I'm somewhere in the middle. I think laptops can be useful, but they also tempt us to multitask. Maybe instead of a total ban, professors could have a 'laptop-free zone' at the front of the lecture hall, so students who want to focus without screens can sit there.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: That's a good compromise. But I still think many students would benefit from putting the laptop away. Studies show that handwritten notes help with memory and understanding. When you type, you tend to transcribe verbatim without processing the information.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: I've heard that too, but it depends on the person. I actually summarize and paraphrase as I type. It's not just mindless copying. And for students with disabilities, laptops are essential.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: Right, accessibility is important. So a blanket ban wouldn't be fair. Perhaps professors could encourage active note-taking strategies rather than banning devices. They could share outlines before class so students don't feel the need to write everything down.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: That could work. And they could use more interactive activities like group discussions or quick quizzes to keep everyone engaged, whether they have a laptop or not.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: I'd be okay with that. As long as I can use my laptop when I need it, and the professor makes the class engaging enough that I won't want to check social media.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: So we agree: no total ban, but better classroom management and optional screen-free zones. Let's suggest that to the department.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: I think we should also consider that some professors might worry about students using laptops for non-academic purposes during exams or quizzes if they are allowed to keep them open.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: That's a valid concern, but most exams are already paper-based or proctored online, so it's not a huge issue.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: True, and we could propose that professors set clear expectations at the start of each class about when laptop use is appropriate and when it isn't.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Good idea. That way, students know the rules and can't claim ignorance.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: Exactly. Clear policies and engaging lectures are the key, not an outright ban.

questions.narration: You will hear three people having a discussion about the challenges of university life.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: There are a lot of challenges for us at university. It’s not just doing well in the courses; we have to be able to balance the academic work with a personal life and also find time to join some extracurricular activities. I mean I don’t want my years at university to be only studying and writing papers.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: I know. There’s just so much to do. I have to get to the lectures, do all the readings and assignments, complete several projects and get ready for exams. I hardly have time to breathe.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: You know, it’s true. My biggest challenge since I started university is managing my time. I can’t seem to get myself organized and I always feel stressed and exhausted and the worst thing is that I just seem to get organized and the term ends and I have to get used to a whole new schedule.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: I agree. That is really difficult. Each course has its own schedule, deadlines and requirements. It’s so difficult to create a consistent routine so I can allocate my time effectively and everything seems to take longer than I thought.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: The worst part is that I often procrastinate and put off tasks until the last minute. I think to myself, oh I have lots of time for that. I have a whole week before it’s due. Then all of a sudden, the due date is in two days and I’m rushed and don’t do a very good job. S1 = Speaker 1, S2 = Speaker 2, S3 = Speaker 3 Please continue transcript on following page.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: If I could manage my time better, I probably wouldn’t be so stressed and exhausted. I’ve never had to discipline myself like this before.
